So it seems the speculation was accurate; Fallout 4 will have a voiced protagonist for the first time in the main series' history.

I was quite excited to see just about every other aspect of the game that Bethesda showed us today, but the voiced protagonist took the wind out of my sails a bit. I would say that the very nature of the voiced protagonist limits dialogue, to an extent. Fallout 2 is one of my favourite games of all time, and that's largely due to the sheer variety of dialogue that the game offers. If you want to be a sincere and cheerful person, you can. If you want to be wryly sarcastic, you can do that too. If you want to trade movie references with an angry enclave dispatcher, you can do that as well. Adding the voice, though, seems to have caused fallout 4 to drop it's number of dialogue options, though. We can see from the trailer that each line the protagonist speaks must be chosen from one of four options. Even Fallout 3, which I would say had the lowest quality character interaction in the series, could have six or more potential options at once.

Beyond that, there exists the other problem that the option you pick may not necessarily represent what your character actually says. A one word summery of a sentence can be misleading. In Mass Effect, for instance, Ashley Williams at one point is talking about her grandfather's disgrace in a previous war, to which one of the options is "I see". You might reasonably expect that option to be a simple "I think I understand your views on aliens a little better" or something to that effect, but picking that option instead leads Shepard to call her grandfather a coward. Another, though probably more intentional, example of this occurs near the beginning of The Witcher 2, where Roche offers a handshake to the bound Geralt. One of his options is "Very funny", which leads Geralt to say, "Fuck you".

That's not to say voiced protagonists are always bad, of course. I mentioned Mass Effect and The Witcher earlier, and indeed I rate both of those series very highly. There is a difference, though, in how a voiced character can be developed versus a silent one. Geralt and Shepard are, to a degree, their own characters (Geralt significantly moreso). No matter what you decide, Geralt will always have the same backstory and the same profession. He will always have a dry wit and be turned off by politics, and he will only ever seriously pursue one of the two women he loves, regardless of whether the player may be interested in somebody else. Shepard is a more open character, but his potentially different backstory and skill class will very rarely be mentioned, and regardless of how the player feels, he will never attempt to surrender to an enemy, or tell Admiral Hackett to piss off and stop calling, or any number of things the player might think to do. I again stress that these are not inherently bad things, but they are certainly a very different experience to what a game like fallout 2 (and similar ones like Planescape: Torment or the more recent Pillars of Eternity) has to offer.

One series to go from standard to the other was Dragon Age. Origins had the older style of the voiceless protagonist (outside of a few canned combat lines, anyway), whereas Dragon Age 2 (and Inquisition) gave a voice to the hero, and in so doing, limited any and all dialogue choices to what would fit on a wheel. This wasn't the only reason Dragon Age 2 was widely panned as an unworthy sequel, and it was perhaps overshadowed by the repetitive environment and enemies, but it was certainly a strong reason to criticise the game all on it's own.

Lastly, a point I thought of while writing that little essay: Fallout games have always been known for making skill checks in dialogue. The beginning of the Old World Blues for Fallout: New Vegas is positively bursting at the seams with opportunities to make use of your character's knowledge of computers, repair skills, awareness, knowledge of explosives, survival skills, intelligence, and so on, and so forth. I can't recall a single game with a voiced protagonist that has used skill checks like this before, and with only four options to work with, I worry that they may be dispensed with entirely.

So that's my rant on the subject over. What do you guys think about the voiced protagonist for Fallout 4?
